name: Heart and great vessels
description: The heart wall, valves and papillary muscles, the coronary arteries and cardiac veins, and the great vessels.

source.attribution: BodyParts3D, (c) The Database Center for Life Science, licensed under CC Attribution-Share Alike 2.1 Japan
source.anatomy_verified: Geometry and identity taken from BodyParts3D (FMA IDs preserved). Shapes simplified for the web only.
source.conversion_notes: Binary STL converted to GLB: vertices welded, meshes simplified with quadric decimation for web delivery, smooth normals, axes converted to Y-up/Z-anterior, recentred, one node per structure. Structures marked "merged" are the union of several BodyParts3D meshes (e.g. the parts of one muscle); structures with a "component" take one connected part of a BodyParts3D mesh, chosen by position.

groups.label: Heart and great vessels
groups.tip: Follow one drop: right atrium, right ventricle, lungs, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta. The right side sends used blood to the lungs, the left sends fresh blood to the body.

groups.label: Heart wall
groups.tip: Say End My Epic for the wall, inside to out: endocardium, myocardium, epicardium. The pericardium is a separate bag around the whole heart.

groups.label: Valves and papillary muscles
groups.tip: Try Pulling My Aorta gives the valve order: tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, aortic. And think LAB RAT: the left inlet valve is bicuspid, the right one tricuspid.

groups.label: Coronary arteries and cardiac veins
groups.tip: The heart's own arteries run in its grooves, each with a vein beside it. Most veins drain into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium.

groups.label: Great vessels
groups.tip: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and veins bring it back. ABC'S names the arch branches, right to left: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian.

content.origin: From the Old English word heorte. The Latin cor and the Greek kardia also mean heart, which is why we call heart things cardiac.
content.location: In the middle of your chest, behind the breastbone and between the lungs, inside a protective sac. About two thirds lies left of the midline, with its tip in the fifth gap between the left ribs.
content.description: This model shows the heart as one wall. Inside are four chambers, two atria on top and two ventricles below, with a dividing wall down the middle. The wall itself has three layers.
content.function: It pumps blood in two loops: the right side sends it to your lungs, and the left side sends it round your body. The left ventricle has the thickest muscle for that big job.
content.mnemonic: Blood order: right atrium, right ventricle, lungs, left atrium, left ventricle. For the three wall layers, say End My Epic: endocardium, myocardium, epicardium.
content.clinical: In a heart attack, a blocked heart artery starves part of the muscle wall. That part dies and can no longer squeeze properly.
content.hint: Find the big muscular pump in the middle of the chest, tip pointing down and left, with large vessels leaving its top.

questions.text: Which chamber receives low-oxygen blood from the two big veins, the superior and inferior venae cavae?
questions.explanation: Both venae cavae empty into the right atrium, the heart's collecting room for blood coming back from the body.

questions.text: What is the correct order of blood flow through the heart?
options: Right atrium, left atrium, lungs, right ventricle, left ventricle
Right atrium, right ventricle, lungs, left atrium, left ventricle
Left atrium, left ventricle, lungs, right atrium, right ventricle
Right ventricle, right atrium, lungs, left ventricle, left atrium
questions.explanation: Blood goes through the right side to the lungs, then back to the left side to be pumped round the body.

questions.text: Which chamber has the thickest muscle wall?
questions.explanation: The left ventricle pumps blood around your whole body, so it needs the thickest, strongest wall.

questions.text: What is the middle, muscle layer of the heart wall called?
questions.explanation: Myo means muscle. The myocardium is the thick muscle layer between the inner endocardium and the outer epicardium.

questions.text: Which wall separates the right and left ventricles?
questions.explanation: Inter means between, so the interventricular septum is the wall between the two ventricles.

questions.text: Where can you usually feel the tip of the heart beating?
options: Left fifth rib gap, below mid-collarbone
Left second rib gap, by the breastbone
questions.explanation: The tip, or apex, points down and left. It sits in the left fifth gap between the ribs, in line with the middle of the collarbone.

questions.text: Which chamber receives oxygen-rich blood from the pulmonary veins?
questions.explanation: Four pulmonary veins bring fresh, oxygen-rich blood from the lungs into the left atrium.

content.origin: From the Latin tri, meaning three, and cuspis, meaning point. It is a valve with three flaps.
content.location: On the right side of the heart, between the right atrium above and the right ventricle below.
content.description: Three thin flaps, like the door flaps of a tent. Fine cords called chordae tendineae, or heartstrings, tie them to small muscles below.
content.function: It opens to let blood drop from the right atrium into the right ventricle, then snaps shut as the ventricle squeezes. Its closing, with the mitral valve, makes the lub sound.
content.mnemonic: Try before you buy: blood passes the tricuspid before the bicuspid. And tRIcuspid is on the RIght.
content.clinical: In people who inject drugs, heart valve infection most often hits this valve. The damaged valve can then leak backward.
content.hint: Find the three-flap gate between the two chambers on the right side.

questions.text: The tricuspid valve lies between which two chambers?
questions.explanation: It is the valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle, the inlet valve on the right side.

questions.text: The tricuspid and mitral valves closing together makes which heart sound?
questions.explanation: The lub is the two inlet valves snapping shut as the ventricles start to squeeze.

content.origin: From the Latin pulmo, meaning lung. It is the doorway to the lungs.
content.location: At the exit of the right ventricle, where blood leaves for the lungs. It sits in front of and a little to the left of the aortic valve.
content.description: Three half-moon shaped pockets with no cords holding them. They fill with blood and press together to seal.
content.function: It opens as the right ventricle squeezes, sending blood toward the lungs, then shuts to stop it falling back. Its closing, with the aortic valve, makes the dub sound.
content.mnemonic: Half-moon valves guard the exits, and flap valves guard the entrances. The pulmonary and aortic valves are the half moons.
content.clinical: Pulmonary valve stenosis, a narrowed valve, is a common heart problem that babies are born with. It makes the right ventricle work harder.
content.hint: Find the half-moon pockets guarding the outflow from the right ventricle to the lungs.

questions.text: Blood passes through the pulmonary valve going from where to where?
questions.explanation: It guards the exit from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk, the big vessel to the lungs.

content.origin: Named after a bishop's tall hat, the mitre. Its two flaps look like the two points of the hat.
content.location: On the left side, between the left atrium and the left ventricle. The aortic valve, not shown separately, sits just in front and to its right.
content.description: Two flaps, one in front and one behind, tied by fine cords to muscles in the left ventricle wall.
content.function: It lets oxygen-rich blood flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle. Then it shuts, so the blood can only leave through the aortic valve.
content.mnemonic: A bishop's mitre has two points, and so does the mitral valve. That is why it is also called the bicuspid valve.
content.clinical: If the mitral valve flops back or leaks, blood escapes back into the left atrium. A doctor hears this as a murmur, loudest over the heart's tip.
content.hint: Find the two-flap valve on the left side, shaped like a bishop's hat.

questions.text: Which is another name for the mitral valve?
questions.explanation: The mitral valve has two flaps, or cusps, so it is also called the bicuspid valve.

questions.text: After the mitral valve, blood fills the left ventricle. Which valve does it leave the heart through?
questions.explanation: The left ventricle pumps blood out through the aortic valve into the aorta.

content.origin: From the Latin papilla, meaning nipple. These muscles stick out from the wall like little nipples.
content.location: Inside the right ventricle, standing out from its inner wall.
content.description: Usually three cone-shaped muscles. From their tips, fine cords run up to the flaps of the tricuspid valve, like the lines of a parachute.
content.function: They tighten as the ventricle squeezes, pulling on the cords. This stops the tricuspid flaps flipping back into the right atrium.
content.mnemonic: Three muscles on the right for the three-flap tricuspid valve.
content.clinical: If these muscles or their cords are damaged, the valve they hold can leak backward.
content.hint: Find the small muscle cones inside the right lower chamber, tied to the three-flap valve by fine cords.

questions.text: What is the main job of papillary muscles?
options: Stop inlet valve flaps flipping into the atria
Carry electrical signals to the atria
questions.explanation: They pull on the cords like parachute lines, so the valve flaps do not flip back into the atria.

content.origin: Latin papilla means nipple. They are named for their small, rounded shape.
content.location: Inside the left ventricle, rising from its thick muscular wall.
content.description: Two large muscles, one in front and one behind. Fine cords from each one fan out to both flaps of the mitral valve.
content.function: They squeeze with the left ventricle to keep the mitral flaps shut. That stops them bulging back into the left atrium.
content.mnemonic: Two muscles on the left for the two-flap mitral valve.
content.clinical: After a heart attack, one of these muscles can tear. The mitral valve then suddenly leaks badly, which is an emergency.
content.hint: Find the two muscle cones inside the thick-walled left lower chamber, anchoring the two-flap valve.

questions.text: The left ventricle's papillary muscles attach by fine cords to which valve?
questions.explanation: They anchor both flaps of the mitral valve, the inlet valve of the left ventricle.

content.origin: From the Latin corona, meaning crown. The heart's own arteries circle it like a crown.
content.location: It starts from the right side of the aorta, just above the aortic valve. It runs in the groove between the right atrium and right ventricle, round to the back.
content.description: A medium-sized artery that gives off the right marginal artery. In most people it also gives the artery that runs down the back of the heart.
content.function: It feeds the right atrium and most of the right ventricle. In most people it also feeds the heart's natural pacemaker and its relay station, the SA and AV nodes.
content.mnemonic: Right for rhythm. The right coronary usually feeds both the pacemaker and the relay station.
content.clinical: A blocked right coronary can cause a heart attack on the underside of the heart. It can also slow the heartbeat, because it feeds the pacemaker cells.
content.hint: Find the vessel from the right side of the aorta, running in the groove between the right atrium and right ventricle.

questions.text: In most people, which artery feeds the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, the heart's pacemaker cells?
questions.explanation: The right coronary artery usually supplies both of the heart's key electrical nodes.

content.origin: From the Latin margo, meaning edge. It runs along the edge of the heart.
content.location: Along the sharp lower right edge of the heart, over the right ventricle.
content.description: A branch of the right coronary artery that runs down toward the tip of the heart.
content.function: It feeds the wall of the right ventricle near the heart's lower edge.
content.mnemonic: Marginal means margin. It hugs the heart's right edge like the margin line on a page.
content.clinical: If the right coronary artery blocks, the area fed by this branch can suffer too, adding to damage in the right ventricle.
content.hint: Find the branch of the right coronary vessel running along the sharp lower edge of the right ventricle.

questions.text: The right marginal artery branches from which artery?
questions.explanation: It is a branch of the right coronary artery, running along the heart's right edge.

content.origin: From the Latin inter, meaning between, and ventriculus, meaning little belly. It runs between the two ventricles at the back.
content.location: In the groove between the ventricles on the underside of the heart, the side that rests on the diaphragm. It runs toward the tip.
content.description: In most people it branches from the right coronary artery. In others it comes from the circumflex artery.
content.function: It feeds the back third of the wall between the ventricles, and the nearby walls of both ventricles.
content.mnemonic: Think of it as the back twin of the artery running down the front. Whichever artery gives it off wins the title of dominant.
content.clinical: Doctors call a heart right or left dominant, depending on which artery gives off this branch. Usually it is the right coronary artery.
content.hint: Find the vessel running down the groove between the ventricles on the underside, beside the middle cardiac vein.

questions.text: Where does the posterior interventricular artery run?
options: In the back groove between the ventricles
Inside the wall between the atria
In the front groove between the ventricles
Along the left edge of the heart
questions.explanation: It runs in the back groove between the ventricles, on the underside of the heart that rests on the diaphragm.

content.origin: From the Latin corona, meaning crown, because these arteries wrap around the heart.
content.location: It starts from the left side of the aorta, just above the aortic valve. It slips between the pulmonary trunk and the left atrium's small ear-shaped flap.
content.description: A short, wide trunk, only about one to two centimetres long. It soon splits into the front descending branch and the circumflex branch.
content.function: Through its two branches it feeds most of the left ventricle, the left atrium and the front two thirds of the wall between the ventricles.
content.mnemonic: The left main splits like a Y. One arm goes down the front, and the other circles round the side.
content.clinical: A blocked left main artery threatens most of the left ventricle. It is a medical emergency.
content.hint: Find the short trunk from the left side of the aorta that quickly splits in two, hidden behind the pulmonary trunk.

questions.text: The left main coronary artery splits into which two branches?
questions.explanation: It splits into the anterior interventricular artery, known as the LAD, and the circumflex artery.

content.origin: From the Latin inter, meaning between, and ventriculus, the word for a ventricle. It runs between the ventricles on the front.
content.location: Straight down the front groove between the ventricles, toward the heart's tip. The great cardiac vein runs beside it.
content.description: A branch of the left main coronary artery. It sends side branches over the left ventricle and deep branches into the wall between the ventricles.
content.function: It feeds the front two thirds of the wall between the ventricles, the front of the left ventricle and the heart's tip.
content.mnemonic: LAD stands for left anterior descending: on the left, on the front, going down.
content.clinical: A sudden block here causes a large heart attack on the front of the heart. That is why it is nicknamed the widow maker.
content.hint: Find the vessel running straight down the front groove between the ventricles toward the tip.

questions.text: Which heart artery is nicknamed the widow maker?
questions.explanation: A block in the LAD causes a large heart attack on the front wall, which earned it the nickname widow maker.

content.origin: From the Latin circum, meaning around, and flectere, meaning to bend. It bends around the heart.
content.location: In the groove between the left atrium and left ventricle. It curves round the left edge of the heart to the back.
content.description: A branch of the left main coronary artery. It gives off the left marginal artery.
content.function: It feeds the left atrium and the side and back walls of the left ventricle.
content.mnemonic: Circumflex circles around, like the circumference of a circle.
content.clinical: In some people, called left dominant, it also gives the artery down the back. Then a block here can harm the back of the dividing wall too.
content.hint: Find the branch curving round the left side of the heart, in the groove between the left atrium and ventricle.

questions.text: The circumflex artery runs in which groove?
options: Right groove between atrium and ventricle
Left groove between atrium and ventricle
questions.explanation: It curves round the heart in the left groove between the atrium and ventricle, called the left atrioventricular groove.

content.origin: From the Latin sinus, meaning a hollow or channel, and corona, meaning crown.
content.location: On the back of the heart, in the groove between the left atrium and left ventricle.
content.description: A wide vein channel, about two to five centimetres long. The great, middle and small cardiac veins all pour into it.
content.function: It collects most of the used blood from the heart muscle and empties it into the right atrium, between the inferior vena cava and the tricuspid valve.
content.mnemonic: Sinus sounds like sink. The heart's own veins drain into it.
content.clinical: Doctors can thread a pacemaker wire through it to pace the left ventricle. This helps both sides of a weak heart beat in time.
content.hint: Find the wide vein channel on the back of the heart that most heart veins empty into.

questions.text: Which chamber does the coronary sinus empty into?
questions.explanation: It opens into the right atrium, close to where the inferior vena cava comes in.

content.origin: Great means large, and cardiac comes from kardia, the Greek word for heart.
content.location: It starts near the heart's tip and climbs the front groove beside the LAD. Then it turns left in the groove and wraps round to the back.
content.description: The biggest vein feeding the coronary sinus. On the back of the heart it widens to become the sinus itself.
content.function: It drains blood from the areas the left coronary artery feeds, mainly the front of both ventricles and the dividing wall.
content.mnemonic: The great vein follows the LAD up the front, then the circumflex around the side.
content.clinical: In heart rhythm tests, doctors pass a thin tube through the coronary sinus into this vein. It lets them record electrical signals from the left side of the heart.
content.hint: Find the vein climbing the front groove beside the front artery, then curving round the left side.

questions.text: On the front of the heart, the great cardiac vein runs beside which artery?
questions.explanation: It climbs the front groove between the ventricles, right alongside the LAD.

content.origin: Middle, because it runs up the middle of the heart's back. Cardiac comes from the Greek kardia, meaning heart.
content.location: In the back groove between the ventricles, on the underside of the heart. It runs beside the posterior interventricular artery.
content.description: A vein that starts near the heart's tip and ends in the coronary sinus, close to where the sinus opens.
content.function: It drains blood from the back walls of both ventricles and the back of the dividing wall.
content.mnemonic: Middle vein, middle of the back. It shadows the artery running down the back groove.
content.clinical: Doctors map it with a dye X-ray of the heart veins before placing a pacing wire for the left ventricle.
content.hint: Find the vein in the back groove between the ventricles, running beside the back descending artery.

questions.text: The middle cardiac vein drains into which structure?
questions.explanation: Like most heart veins, it empties into the coronary sinus.

content.origin: From the Greek aorte, linked to a word meaning to lift. It is the great artery lifted up from the heart.
content.location: It starts at the aortic valve of the left ventricle and rises about five centimetres, up and to the right, behind the breastbone.
content.description: Just above the aortic valve are three small bulges, and the two coronary arteries start from two of them. The aortic valve is not shown separately here.
content.function: It carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle up to the arch of the aorta. On the way, it feeds the heart's own arteries first.
content.mnemonic: The heart feeds itself first. The coronary arteries are the very first branches off the aorta.
content.clinical: In aortic stenosis the aortic valve narrows. The left ventricle must push harder, which can cause chest pain, fainting and breathlessness.
content.hint: Find the first part of the body's main artery, rising from the left ventricle and giving off the two heart arteries.

questions.text: Which are the only branches of the ascending aorta?
options: Right and left common carotid arteries
questions.explanation: The right and left coronary arteries start from small bulges just above the aortic valve.

questions.text: The aortic valve lies between which two structures?
questions.explanation: It guards the exit from the left ventricle into the ascending aorta.

content.origin: From the Latin arcus, meaning bow or arch. Aorta comes from the Greek name for the great artery.
content.location: Behind the top of the breastbone. It arches back and to the left over the left lung artery and left main airway, starting and ending level with the sternal angle.
content.description: A curved section shaped like a walking stick handle. Three branches rise from its top, and a small cord ties it to the left lung artery.
content.function: It carries blood from the rising aorta round to the descending aorta. Its three branches send blood to the head, neck and arms.
content.mnemonic: Remember ABC'S: from the Arch come the Brachiocephalic trunk, the left Common carotid and the left Subclavian.
content.clinical: Coarctation is a narrowing of the aorta present from birth, usually near that small cord. It causes high blood pressure in the arms and weak pulses in the legs.
content.hint: Find the curved part of the main artery behind the top of the breastbone, with three branches rising from its top.

questions.text: From right to left, what is the order of branches off the aortic arch?
options: Left subclavian, left common carotid, brachiocephalic trunk
Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian
Right coronary, left coronary, brachiocephalic trunk
Left common carotid, brachiocephalic trunk, left subclavian
questions.explanation: First comes the brachiocephalic trunk, then the left common carotid, then the left subclavian. Think ABC'S.

content.origin: Aorta comes from the Greek for the great artery. Descending comes from the Latin descendere, to go down.
content.location: It runs down the back of the chest, just left of the spine. It passes through the diaphragm at the twelfth thoracic vertebra, T12, to become the abdominal aorta.
content.description: The longest part of the aorta, with a chest part and a belly part. Low in the belly it splits into the two common iliac arteries, about level with L4.
content.function: It carries oxygen-rich blood to the chest wall, belly organs, pelvis and legs through its many branches.
content.mnemonic: Straight down beside the spine: the chest part is above the diaphragm, and the belly part is below.
content.clinical: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is a weak, ballooning section of the aorta in the belly. If it bursts, it causes life-threatening bleeding.
content.hint: Find the long, straight continuation of the main artery running down beside the spine.

questions.text: At which level does the descending aorta pass through the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: It passes through the diaphragm at T12, the twelfth thoracic vertebra, and becomes the abdominal aorta.

content.origin: From the Greek brachion, meaning arm, and kephale, meaning head. It feeds the arm and the head.
content.location: The first and biggest branch of the aortic arch. It rises up and to the right, behind the breastbone handle, to the joint where the right collarbone meets the breastbone.
content.description: A short, wide artery, about four to five centimetres long, with no side branches. At its end it splits in two.
content.function: It carries blood to the right side of the head and neck and to the right arm.
content.mnemonic: One trunk, two veins: there is only one brachiocephalic artery, on the right, but there are two brachiocephalic veins.
content.clinical: It crosses in front of the windpipe low in the neck. Surgeons watch for it when making a breathing hole there, called a tracheostomy, as it can bleed.
content.hint: Find the first, widest branch off the top of the arch, heading toward the right collarbone joint.

questions.text: The brachiocephalic trunk splits into which two arteries?
options: Left subclavian and left common carotid
Right subclavian and right common carotid
questions.explanation: Behind the right collarbone joint it splits into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries.

content.origin: From the Greek karoun, meaning to stupefy. Pressing on these arteries can make a person faint.
content.location: It rises straight from the aortic arch as its second branch. It climbs the left side of the neck beside the windpipe.
content.description: It has no branches in the neck until it splits in two, about level with the top of the Adam's apple.
content.function: It supplies the left side of the head and neck. Its inner branch, the internal carotid, feeds much of the brain.
content.mnemonic: The left carotid comes straight off the arch. The right one comes from the brachiocephalic trunk.
content.clinical: Fatty narrowing of the carotid arteries is a common cause of stroke. You can feel the carotid pulse beside your voice box.
content.hint: Find the middle of the three branches on top of the arch, heading up the left side of the neck.

questions.text: Where does the left common carotid artery start?
options: Directly from the arch of the aorta
questions.explanation: It is the second branch, coming straight off the arch of the aorta.

content.origin: From the Latin sub, meaning under, and clavis, meaning key, as in clavicle. It runs under the collarbone.
content.location: The third and last branch of the aortic arch. It arches over the first rib, under the collarbone, toward the left arm.
content.description: It gives off the vertebral artery and other branches. At the outer edge of the first rib it becomes the axillary artery, the artery of the armpit.
content.function: It supplies the left arm. Through the vertebral artery it also feeds part of the brain, the spinal cord and the neck.
content.mnemonic: Sub-clavian means under the clavicle. Follow the collarbone and you follow this artery.
content.clinical: In subclavian steal syndrome, a narrowing before the vertebral branch lets the working arm steal blood from the brain during arm exercise.
content.hint: Find the last branch off the top of the arch, curving over the first rib toward the left arm.

questions.text: The left subclavian artery mainly supplies which area?
options: Left side of the head only
questions.explanation: It becomes the axillary artery and carries blood down to the left arm.

content.origin: From the Latin pulmo, meaning lung. These vessels lead to the lungs.
content.location: The trunk leaves the right ventricle at the front of the heart, left of the aorta. Under the aortic arch it splits into right and left arteries.
content.description: A short, wide trunk and its two branches, shaped like a Y. The right branch passes behind the ascending aorta and the superior vena cava.
content.function: They carry low-oxygen blood from the right ventricle to the lungs to pick up oxygen. They are the only arteries in adults that carry low-oxygen blood.
content.mnemonic: Arteries go Away from the heart, even when their blood is low in oxygen.
content.clinical: A pulmonary embolism is a clot, usually from a deep leg vein, that lodges here and blocks blood flow to the lungs.
content.hint: Find the trunk from the right ventricle that splits in two under the arch, carrying blood to the lungs.

questions.text: What type of blood do the pulmonary arteries carry?
options: Low-oxygen blood to the coronary sinus
Oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium
questions.explanation: They carry low-oxygen blood from the right ventricle to the lungs to pick up fresh oxygen.

questions.text: A clot from a deep leg vein that lodges in these vessels is called what?
questions.explanation: A pulmonary embolism is a clot blocking the pulmonary arteries, cutting blood flow to the lungs.

content.origin: From the Latin pulmo, meaning lung, and vena, meaning vein. This one comes from the top of the right lung.
content.location: It leaves the upper part of the right lung's root and runs inward to the back of the left atrium, passing behind the superior vena cava and right atrium.
content.description: One of four lung veins, two from each side, with no valves inside. This one drains the upper part of the right lung.
content.function: It carries oxygen-rich blood from the lung to the left atrium. The lung veins are the only veins in adults that carry oxygen-rich blood.
content.mnemonic: Four lung veins, four corners of the left atrium: an upper and a lower vein from each lung.
content.clinical: Stray electrical signals near the lung vein openings often trigger atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat. Ablation treats it by sealing these veins off electrically.
content.hint: Find the upper of the two vessels on the right side entering the back of the left atrium.

questions.text: What do the pulmonary veins carry?
options: Oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium
Oxygen-rich blood to the right ventricle
Low-oxygen blood to the right atrium
questions.explanation: They bring fresh, oxygen-rich blood back from the lungs into the left atrium.

content.origin: Pulmo is Latin for lung and vena is Latin for vein. This vein drains the lower right lung.
content.location: It leaves the lower part of the right lung's root and runs inward to the back of the left atrium. On the way it passes behind the superior vena cava and right atrium.
content.description: A valveless vein, one of four that return blood from the lungs. It drains the lower part of the right lung.
content.function: It brings freshly oxygenated blood from the lower right lung into the left atrium, ready to be pumped round the body.
content.mnemonic: Two up, two down: each lung sends an upper and a lower vein into the left atrium.
content.clinical: The lung vein openings are a common starting point for atrial fibrillation. Ablation makes a ring of scar around them to block the stray signals.
content.hint: Find the lower of the two vessels on the right side entering the back of the left atrium.

questions.text: How many pulmonary veins usually enter the left atrium?
questions.explanation: There are usually four, an upper and a lower vein from each lung.

content.origin: From the Latin pulmo, lung, and vena, vein. It drains the top of the left lung.
content.location: It leaves the upper part of the left lung's root and runs inward to the left side of the back of the left atrium.
content.description: A valveless vein, one of the four lung veins. It carries blood from the upper part of the left lung.
content.function: It returns oxygen-rich blood from the upper left lung to the left atrium. Unusually for a vein, its blood is full of oxygen.
content.mnemonic: Veins come back to the heart. Lung veins come back full of fresh oxygen.
content.clinical: An irregular heartbeat called atrial fibrillation often starts near these vein openings. Catheter ablation cuts them off electrically to calm the rhythm.
content.hint: Find the upper of the two vessels on the left side entering the back of the left atrium.

questions.text: Catheter ablation around the pulmonary vein openings treats which condition?
questions.explanation: Stray signals near the lung veins often trigger atrial fibrillation, so ablation isolates the veins.

content.origin: Latin pulmo means lung and vena means vein. This is the lower vein from the left lung.
content.location: It leaves the lower part of the left lung's root and runs inward to the left side of the back of the left atrium.
content.description: The lower of the two left lung veins, with no valves inside. It drains the lower part of the left lung.
content.function: It carries oxygen-rich blood from the lower left lung into the left atrium. Lung veins are the only adult veins that carry oxygen-rich blood.
content.mnemonic: Arteries go away and veins come back, whatever their blood. Lung veins come back bright red with oxygen.
content.clinical: Like the other lung veins, its opening can spark atrial fibrillation. Ablation isolates it to stop the irregular rhythm.
content.hint: Find the lower of the two vessels on the left side entering the back of the left atrium.

questions.text: The pulmonary veins are unusual because they are veins that carry what?
questions.explanation: In adults, the pulmonary veins are the only veins that carry oxygen-rich blood.

content.origin: From the Latin vena cava, meaning hollow vein. Superior means upper.
content.location: On the right of the upper chest, beside the ascending aorta. It forms behind the right first rib cartilage and runs down into the right atrium.
content.description: A large vein with no valves, about seven centimetres long. It forms where the right and left brachiocephalic veins join.
content.function: It brings low-oxygen blood from the head, neck, arms and chest wall back to the right atrium.
content.mnemonic: The superior vena cava brings blood from above the heart. The inferior vena cava brings it from below.
content.clinical: If something presses on this vein, often a lung cancer or lymphoma, blood backs up. The face, neck and arms swell, and the neck veins bulge.
content.hint: Find the large vein to the right of the ascending aorta, formed by two veins joining and draining down into the right atrium.

questions.text: The superior vena cava forms where which veins join?
options: Right and left common iliac veins
questions.explanation: The right and left brachiocephalic veins join behind the right first rib cartilage to form it.

content.origin: From the Latin vena cava, meaning hollow vein. Inferior means lower.
content.location: It climbs the back of the belly, to the right of the aorta. It passes through the diaphragm at T8, the eighth thoracic vertebra, and enters the bottom of the right atrium.
content.description: The largest vein in the body. It forms low in the belly, about level with L5, where the two common iliac veins join.
content.function: It brings low-oxygen blood from the legs, pelvis and belly back to the right atrium.
content.mnemonic: I 8 10 Eggs At 12: the vena cava crosses the diaphragm at T8, the oesophagus at T10 and the aorta at T12.
content.clinical: Late in pregnancy, lying flat on the back lets the womb press on this vein. Less blood returns to the heart, and blood pressure can drop.
content.hint: Find the largest vein, rising through the diaphragm to enter the right atrium from below.

questions.text: At which level does the inferior vena cava pass through the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: It passes through its own opening in the diaphragm at T8, the eighth thoracic vertebra.

content.origin: From the Greek brachion, meaning arm, and kephale, meaning head. It drains the arm and the head.
content.location: Behind the joint where the right collarbone meets the breastbone. It runs almost straight down on the right side of the upper chest.
content.description: A short vein, about two and a half centimetres long. It forms where the right internal jugular and right subclavian veins join.
content.function: It drains the right side of the head and neck and the right arm. It then joins the left brachiocephalic vein to form the superior vena cava.
content.mnemonic: Right is short and straight. Left is long and crosses over.
content.clinical: A central line placed in the right internal jugular vein runs down through this vein into the superior vena cava.
content.hint: Find the short upright vein behind the right collarbone joint, where the neck and arm veins meet.

questions.text: Each brachiocephalic vein forms where which two veins join?
questions.explanation: The internal jugular vein from the neck and the subclavian vein from the arm join behind the collarbone joint.

questions.text: Which brachiocephalic vein is longer and crosses behind the manubrium?
questions.explanation: The left one is longer, because it has to cross behind the breastbone handle to reach the right side.

content.origin: Greek brachion means arm and kephale means head. It collects blood from the left arm and the left side of the head.
content.location: It starts behind the left collarbone joint and slants across to the right, behind the breastbone handle and in front of the arch's branches.
content.description: About six centimetres long, more than twice as long as the right one. It forms where the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins join.
content.function: It drains the left side of the head and neck and the left arm into the superior vena cava.
content.mnemonic: Picture a long diagonal bridge across the top of the arch. That bridge is the left brachiocephalic vein.
content.clinical: It lies just behind the breastbone handle. A crushing chest injury, or surgery through the breastbone, can damage it.
content.hint: Find the long diagonal vein crossing from left to right behind the breastbone handle, above the arch.
